```{python}
#| include: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from modelperf.data import CLAIM_AMOUNT_CAP, FEATURES, housing_split, train_test
from modelperf.models import binary_predictions, housing_predictions, pure_premium_predictions

split = train_test()
policies = pd.concat([split.train, split.test])
n_policies = f"{len(policies):,}"
n_test = f"{len(split.test):,}"
claim_rate = f"{policies['HasClaim'].mean():.1%}"
share_zero = f"{(policies['PurePremium'] == 0).mean():.1%}"
```

## French motor insurance (freMTPL2)

The dataset comes from a French insurer and is published on
[OpenML](https://www.openml.org/d/41214) in two tables: one row per policy
(risk features and exposure) and one row per claim (claim amount). It
contains `{python} n_policies` policies.

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `Area`, `Region` | Where the policyholder lives |
| `Density` | Inhabitants per km² in the policyholder's city |
| `DrivAge` | Age of the driver |
| `BonusMalus` | Bonus-malus level: below 100 means a claim-free history, above 100 a surcharge |
| `VehPower`, `VehAge`, `VehBrand`, `VehGas` | Vehicle power, age, brand and fuel |
| `Exposure` | Fraction of a year the policy was in force (≤ 1) |

### Targets

**`HasClaim` (binary).** 1 if the policy had at least one claim during its
exposure period, 0 otherwise. Only `{python} claim_rate` of policies had a
claim, so the classes are heavily imbalanced, which is typical for real
classification problems and important for how metrics behave.

**`PurePremium` (continuous).** Total claim cost divided by exposure, i.e. the
cost per policy-year. It's what an insurer has to charge (before expenses) to
cover claims. `{python} share_zero` of policies have a pure premium of 0, and
the rest have a long right tail. Because pure premium is a rate per year, a
policy observed for a full year carries more information than one observed for
a week. All pure-premium models and metrics are therefore **weighted by
exposure**.

::: {.callout-note}
## Data preparation
- The claim count is taken from the claims table, so `HasClaim` and
  `PurePremium` always agree.
- Total claim cost per policy is capped at `{python} f"{CLAIM_AMOUNT_CAP:,}"` EUR
  (a few claims reach 4 million), and exposure is capped at 1 year.
- Average cost per claim ('severity') was considered as a target and dropped:
  in this dataset, no model predicts it better than the overall mean.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-targets
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of the two targets."
pp = policies.loc[policies["PurePremium"] > 0, "PurePremium"]
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Statistic": ["Policies", "Claim rate", "Share with pure premium 0",
                      "Median pure premium (when > 0)", "99th percentile (when > 0)"],
        "Value": [n_policies, claim_rate, share_zero,
                  f"{pp.median():,.0f} EUR", f"{pp.quantile(0.99):,.0f} EUR"],
    }
)
```

### Train/test split

Policies are split once into 75% training and 25% test data
(`{python} n_test` policies), stratified on `HasClaim` so both parts have the
same claim rate. **Every metric in this project is computed on the test set.**
Performance on the training data says how well a model memorized it, not how
it will perform on new policies.

## California Housing

A classic regression dataset (shipped with scikit-learn): the median house
value of 20,640 Californian districts from the 1990 census, in units of
100,000 USD, with 8 features such as median income, house age and location.
Unlike pure premium, it has a strong, smooth signal, so we use it to show how
error metrics behave in the textbook case. It has one quirk: values were
capped at 5.0 when the data was collected, which shows up in the residual
plots.

## Models

Every target gets the same three models:

| Model | `HasClaim` | `PurePremium` | California Housing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Null** | training claim rate | training mean (exposure-weighted) | training mean |
| **GLM** | logistic regression | Tweedie GLM, power 1.9, log link | linear regression |
| **GBM** | gradient boosting, log loss | gradient boosting, Poisson loss | gradient boosting, squared error |

- **Null** is the 'no model' reference. Any metric value only means something
  next to what the Null model achieves.
- **GLM** is the traditional, interpretable baseline, still the standard in
  insurance pricing. The insurance GLMs use one-hot encoded categoricals,
  binned vehicle and driver age, and log-scaled density and bonus-malus.
- **GBM** (`HistGradientBoosting` in scikit-learn) is the flexible challenger.
  It handles the categorical features natively and stops adding trees when a
  validation split stops improving.

The models are deliberately reasonable but not heavily tuned: the project is
about *measuring* performance, not maximizing it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "Average test-set prediction of each model next to the actual average."
b, p, h = binary_predictions(), pure_premium_predictions(), housing_predictions()
rows = {
    "HasClaim (claim rate)": [b["y"].mean()] + [b[m].mean() for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")],
    "PurePremium (EUR/year)": [np.average(p["y"], weights=p["w"])]
        + [np.average(p[m], weights=p["w"]) for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")],
    "House value (100k USD)": [h["y"].mean()] + [h[m].mean() for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")],
}
pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["Actual", "Null", "GLM", "GBM"]).T.round(4)
```

Here is how to get these predictions in your own code:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from modelperf.models import binary_predictions

b = binary_predictions()  # columns: y, Null, GLM, GBM (one row per test policy)
```
